blocks.title: Oscillatory motion
blocks.text: Oscillatory motion is a to-and-fro motion about a mean position. It is a periodic motion, which repeats itself after equal intervals of time.

items: A simple pendulum displaced from its rest position.
A mass on the end of a spring, in a horizontal or vertical plane, when pulled and released.
The atoms or molecules of a solid oscillating about their mean positions.
Air molecules when sound waves travel through air.
The strings of musical instruments such as the guitar and violin.

blocks.text: Every body that vibrates or oscillates has an equilibrium (mean) position. When it is displaced from this position, a restoring force acts to bring it back, and this causes the vibration or oscillation.

items: Vibration: one complete round trip (cycle) of a vibrating body about its mean position; for example, the bob of a pendulum moving from A to B and back to A.
Instantaneous displacement (x): the distance of the vibrating body from its mean position at any instant.

Amplitude (xo): the magnitude of the maximum displacement on either side of the mean position. For a wave, the amplitude measures the energy carried: the greater the amplitude, the greater the energy.
Time period (T): the time taken to complete one vibration; SI unit the second (s). T = 1/f = 2 pi / w.
Frequency (f): the number of vibrations completed in one second, f = n/t = 1/T. Its unit is the hertz (Hz), one oscillation per second; its dimension is [T^-1].
Angular frequency (w): the angular displacement per unit time, w = theta/t. For one revolution theta = 2 pi radians in time T, so w = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f. Its SI unit is rad s^-1.

blocks.alt: Left: a simple pendulum hangs from a support; the bob is drawn at the mean position O and, dashed, at the extreme positions A and B, with a curved path between them. A red arrow from O to B is labelled amplitude xo = OB, and a note says one vibration is A to B to A. blocks.long_description: The bob swings between two extreme positions an equal distance either side of O. The amplitude is measured from O to one extreme, not from one extreme to the other.
